views.name: orders_core
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  order_id,
  customer_id,
  order_status,
  order_purchase_timestamp,
  order_approved_at,
  order_delivered_carrier_date,
  order_delivered_customer_date,
  order_estimated_delivery_date,
  -- derived normalized timestamps as ISO strings (preserve original columns too)
  CASE WHEN order_purchase_timestamp = '' THEN NULL ELSE order_purchase_timestamp END AS order_purchase_timestamp_normalized,
  CASE WHEN order_approved_at = '' THEN NULL ELSE order_approved_at END AS order_approved_at_normalized,
  CASE WHEN order_delivered_carrier_date = '' THEN NULL ELSE order_delivered_carrier_date END AS order_delivered_carrier_date_normalized,
  CASE WHEN order_delivered_customer_date = '' THEN NULL ELSE order_delivered_customer_date END AS order_delivered_customer_date_normalized,
  CASE WHEN order_estimated_delivery_date = '' THEN NULL ELSE order_estimated_delivery_date END AS order_estimated_delivery_date_normalized
FROM olist_orders

params.description: One-row-per-order core view: returns order-level identifiers, order status, original timestamp fields, and 'normalized' timestamp fields (empty-string -> NULL) for analysis of order lifecycle and joins to other order-level data.
params.when_to_use: Getting one record per order to analyze order status, purchase/approval/delivery/estimated timestamps. | Joining order-level attributes (order_id, customer_id, order_status, timestamps) to customer, payment-aggregates, or order-item aggregates when you need the canonical order grain. | Computing time-to-approval, time-to-delivery, or filtering orders by purchase/approved/delivered timestamps.
params.when_not_to_use: Joining directly to order_items_core or payments_core without aggregation: these are one-to-many relative to orders (order_items_core has multiple rows per order_id, payments_core may have multiple payments per order_id). Doing so will multiply order rows and silently inflate counts or sums. | Using this view to compute order-level metrics by simply summing child-table rows after an un-aggregated join (mis-count): e.g., SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders_core JOIN order_items_core USING(order_id) will count order-item rows, not orders. | Attempting cohort-level analyses that require stable cohort assignment per row but joining on non-unique keys (e.g., joining sellers or items without aggregating) — this can break the one-row-per-order grain and produce incorrect cohort sizes. | Treating the *_normalized columns as having changed datatype or timezone conversion: they only replace empty-string with NULL and otherwise preserve original string values; they are not parsed/converted to timestamps.
params.output_schema: order_id: unique order identifier at the order grain; derived directly from olist_orders.order_id | customer_id: identifier of the customer who placed the order; derived directly from olist_orders.customer_id | order_status: current status label for the order (e.g., delivered, shipped); derived directly from olist_orders.order_status | order_purchase_timestamp: original purchase timestamp string as stored in olist_orders.order_purchase_timestamp | order_approved_at: original approval timestamp string as stored in olist_orders.order_approved_at | order_delivered_carrier_date: original carrier delivery date string as stored in olist_orders.order_delivered_carrier_date | order_delivered_customer_date: original customer delivery date string as stored in olist_orders.order_delivered_customer_date | order_estimated_delivery_date: original estimated delivery date string as stored in olist_orders.order_estimated_delivery_date | order_purchase_timestamp_normalized: same as order_purchase_timestamp but empty-string mapped to NULL; expression: CASE WHEN order_purchase_timestamp = '' THEN NULL ELSE order_purchase_timestamp END | order_approved_at_normalized: same as order_approved_at but empty-string mapped to NULL; expression: CASE WHEN order_approved_at = '' THEN NULL ELSE order_approved_at END | order_delivered_carrier_date_normalized: same as order_delivered_carrier_date but empty-string mapped to NULL; expression: CASE WHEN order_delivered_carrier_date = '' THEN NULL ELSE order_delivered_carrier_date END | order_delivered_customer_date_normalized: same as order_delivered_customer_date but empty-string mapped to NULL; expression: CASE WHEN order_delivered_customer_date = '' THEN NULL ELSE order_delivered_customer_date END | order_estimated_delivery_date_normalized: same as order_estimated_delivery_date but empty-string mapped to NULL; expression: CASE WHEN order_estimated_delivery_date = '' THEN NULL ELSE order_estimated_delivery_date END
params.grounded_columns: olist_orders.order_id | olist_orders.customer_id | olist_orders.order_status | olist_orders.order_purchase_timestamp | olist_orders.order_approved_at | olist_orders.order_delivered_carrier_date | olist_orders.order_delivered_customer_date | olist_orders.order_estimated_delivery_date
params.metric: This view is strictly descriptive at the order grain and does not define aggregated metrics. Derived columns = normalization expressions mapping empty-string to NULL, e.g.: order_purchase_timestamp_normalized = CASE WHEN order_purchase_timestamp = '' THEN NULL ELSE order_purchase_timestamp END | No aggregates (COUNT/SUM/AVG) are computed in this view; downstream metrics must aggregate at order-level explicitly and beware of join-induced duplication.
params.composition: Cardinality-SAFE joins (do not duplicate measures): |  - Join to customers_core on orders_core.customer_id = customers_core.customer_id — safe because customers_core is one-row-per-customer (a dimension), which will not duplicate order rows. |  - Join to sellers_core when joining via a pre-aggregated seller-level table keyed by seller_id (one-row-per-seller) — but do not join directly to order_items_core/sellers without aggregation (see below). | Unsafe joins (will duplicate this view's rows/measures unless you aggregate first): |  - Do NOT directly join to order_items_core on order_id without aggregating order_items_core to order-level (e.g., sum(quantity) or count(items) grouped by order_id). order_items_core is one-to-many to orders_core; an un-aggregated join will duplicate orders and inflate counts/sums. |  - Do NOT directly join to payments_core on order_id without first aggregating payments to order-level (e.g., total_paid per order). payments_core can be multi-row per order. |  - Do NOT join to product-level tables (products_core) via order_items_core without aggregating order_items_core, because product joins through items multiply rows. | Guidance for correct composition: always preserve order grain by either (a) joining only to one-to-one/one-to-few dimension tables keyed by customer_id or other unique keys, or (b) pre-aggregating any one-to-many child (items, payments, reviews) to order_id before joining back to orders_core.
params.comparison: use orders_with_items_payments instead when you need item- or payment-level detail at the order row because orders_with_items_payments is a join view that combines orders with items and payments (but be aware that it may expand rows per item/payment). | use customer_order_counts when you need pre-computed aggregated metrics per customer (customer-level order counts) rather than raw order rows — customer_order_counts is an AGG view providing customer-level aggregates. | use latest_review_per_order when you specifically need one review per order (it applies ranking to reviews) so you can safely join reviews to orders without duplicating order rows. | use order_review_summary when you need aggregated review metrics per order — it returns order-level aggregates and is safe to join to orders_core without causing row multiplication.

views.description: Canonicalized order-level relation: one row per order with parsed timestamps and key order status and customer reference. Use for joining to payments/items/reviews or for time-based analyses. | Use for: order lifecycle timelines; orders by status or purchase date; join-ready orders for aggregation with items/payments/reviews

views.name: order_items_core
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  order_id,
  order_item_id,
  product_id,
  seller_id,
  shipping_limit_date,
  price,
  freight_value
FROM olist_order_items

params.description: Provides one row per order item with its product, seller, shipping limit date, price and freight value — useful for item-level revenue and fulfillment analyses.
params.when_to_use: Calculate item-level revenue, freight costs, or item counts by product/seller/order. | Join item attributes to product or seller dimensions when you need details at the order_item granularity. | Filter or segment orders by item-level fields such as product_id, seller_id, shipping_limit_date, price, or freight_value.
params.when_not_to_use: Aggregating to order-level totals without first aggregating this view — because this view is grain ['order_id','order_item_id']; naively joining and then aggregating elsewhere can double-count if joined to other one-to-many tables. | Using it as a cohort (customer- or order-level) anchor directly — cohorts defined at customer/order level should use customers_core or orders_core to avoid mixing granularities. | Joining to another one-to-many table (e.g., payments or reviews) without re-aggregation — this will multiply rows and produce silently wrong sums/counts. | Treating price or freight_value as pre-aggregated metrics across an order — these are per-item values; summing them gives order totals, but treating a single row as an order total is an error.
params.output_schema: order_id: identifier of the order this item belongs to — derived from olist_order_items.order_id | order_item_id: identifier of the item within the order — derived from olist_order_items.order_item_id | product_id: product identifier for this item — derived from olist_order_items.product_id | seller_id: seller identifier responsible for this item — derived from olist_order_items.seller_id | shipping_limit_date: promised latest shipping date for this item (datetime) — derived from olist_order_items.shipping_limit_date | price: unit price charged for this order item (numeric) — derived from olist_order_items.price | freight_value: shipping cost charged for this order item (numeric) — derived from olist_order_items.freight_value
params.grounded_columns: olist_order_items.order_id | olist_order_items.order_item_id | olist_order_items.product_id | olist_order_items.seller_id | olist_order_items.shipping_limit_date | olist_order_items.price | olist_order_items.freight_value
params.metric: price = olist_order_items.price | freight_value = olist_order_items.freight_value | order_item_revenue = price  -- treat as per-row (per item) revenue; to get order-level revenue SUM(price) grouped by order_id | order_item_shipping = freight_value  -- treat as per-row (per item) shipping; to get order-level shipping SUM(freight_value) grouped by order_id
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to products_core on product_id — safe because products_core is one-row-per-product_id, so it does not duplicate order_items rows. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to sellers_core on seller_id — safe because sellers_core is one-row-per-seller_id, so it does not duplicate order_items rows. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to customers_core only via orders_core (orders_core -> customers_core) when you aggregate to order level first — direct join of order_items to customers_core requires joining order_items.order_id -> orders_core.order_id (one-to-one per order) then orders_core.customer_id -> customers_core (one-to-one per customer) to avoid multiplicity. | do NOT join directly to payments_core without aggregation: payments_core may contain multiple payment rows per order_id (different payment attempts/types); joining payments_core to this view will multiply rows and over-count price/freight unless you first aggregate payments to one row per order_id (e.g., SUM or an agreed selection). | do NOT join directly to order_review_summary or latest_review_per_order without ensuring one-row-per-order join keys: reviews are one-per-order in some sibling views (e.g., latest_review_per_order) but multi-review sources must be reduced; otherwise metrics like SUM(price) will be inflated. | when combining with geolocation_zip_median (aggregated by zip), ensure you join via the order -> customer -> geolocation path at the appropriate grain and re-aggregate the item metrics after the join to avoid duplicating item rows for multiple geolocation matches.
params.comparison: use orders_core instead when you need order-level attributes or to anchor analyses at the order grain — orders_core has one row per order and avoids per-item duplication when computing order-level cohorts or funnels. | use customers_core when the analysis is customer-centric (customer lifetime value, cohorts) because customer-level views already collapse orders/items to the customer grain. | use products_core when you only need product attributes and not item-level price/freight values — products_core is product-grain and may include product master attributes missing from this transactional view. | use orders_with_items_payments when you need pre-joined order+item+payment data (convenience) — that sibling handles some join/aggregation concerns; prefer it if it matches your required grain to avoid doing unsafe joins yourself.

views.description: One row per order item with price and freight measures, preserving product and seller keys. Use as basis for item-level revenue, seller performance and product analyses. | Use for: item-level revenue and freight analysis; per-seller or per-product aggregates; shipping deadline vs delivery timing when joined with orders

views.name: payments_core
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  order_id,
  payment_sequential,
  payment_type,
  payment_installments,
  payment_value
FROM olist_order_payments

params.description: Provides one row per payment for each order: payment identifiers and payment-level attributes (type, installments, value).
params.when_to_use: When you need payment-level details (e.g., analyze payment types, installments, or payment amounts) for each order payment instance. | When joining payments onto order-level or item-level records where payments should remain at their native payment-per-order grain. | When computing aggregates over payments (sum of payment_value, counts of payment records) using this view as the source of truth for payment rows.
params.when_not_to_use: Joining this view to item-level data and then summing payment_value without re-aggregation — WRONG because order_items is one-to-many per order and will duplicate payment rows, inflating payment_value. | Using this view directly to compute customer-level payment totals without grouping by customer (or joining to an orders view and then aggregating properly) — WRONG because payments are per order and must be rolled up explicitly to customer granularity. | Treating payment_sequential as a cohort or timeline dimension across orders (for example, assuming payment_sequential = 1 always corresponds to first payment across the dataset) — WRONG because payment_sequential is sequential per order_id, not globally comparable across orders. | Joining to another payments-like table (if present) that also stores multiple rows per (order_id, payment_sequential) without a clear key match — WRONG because mismatched multiplicities can silently duplicate or drop payment rows.
params.output_schema: order_id: order identifier — directly from olist_order_payments.order_id. Use to join back to order-level tables. | payment_sequential: payment sequence number within the order — directly from olist_order_payments.payment_sequential. Indicates the nth payment record for that order. | payment_type: payment method/type (e.g., credit card, boleto) — directly from olist_order_payments.payment_type. | payment_installments: number of installments for this payment — directly from olist_order_payments.payment_installments. | payment_value: monetary amount of this payment record — directly from olist_order_payments.payment_value. This is a payment-level measure; aggregate with SUM when rolling up.
params.metric: payment_value = payment_value (payment-level measure; to aggregate to higher grain use SUM(payment_value) grouped by desired key) | payment_count = COUNT(*) when counting payment rows (group by desired key) | distinct_payments_per_order = COUNT(payment_sequential) GROUP BY order_id (if you need number of payment rows per order)
params.composition: Safe: join to orders_core on order_id — safe because orders_core is one-row-per-order_id, so joining will not duplicate payment rows (payments are one-or-many per order; join preserves payment grain). | Safe: join to customers_core via orders_core (payments -> orders_core -> customers_core) — safe if you join payments -> orders_core (1-to-many: order to payments) then orders_core -> customers_core (1-to-1 on customer_id). Aggregation to customer-level must still be explicit (SUM(payment_value) GROUP BY customer_id). | Do NOT join directly to order_items_core without re-aggregation — order_items_core is one-to-many per order_id and will multiply payment rows, causing inflated SUM(payment_value). If you must combine payments with items, either: (a) aggregate payments to order_id first (SUM(payment_value) GROUP BY order_id) and join that aggregated result to order_items_core, or (b) aggregate items to order_id first before joining. | Do NOT join to sibling JOIN views that already combine orders with multiple child rows (e.g., orders_with_items_payments) unless you understand their grain — joining this payments view to a multi-row-per-order pre-joined view will likely produce duplicates. Prefer joining to single-row-per-order dimensions or to aggregated payment results. | When joining to geolocation_zip_median, product_category_translation, seller_revenue_rolling, or other AGG/WIN views: confirm their grain. If they are per-order (or per-order_id) it's safe; if they are per-item or per-seller and one-to-many relative to payments' keys, re-aggregate appropriately before joining.
params.comparison: use orders_with_items_payments when you need a pre-joined dataset combining orders, items and payments in a specific denormalized shape — it may already handle multiplicity and aggregation. payments_core should be used when you need raw, canonical payment rows. | use orders_core instead when you need pure order-level attributes (single row per order). payments_core differs because it has multiple rows per order when multiple payments exist. | use customer_order_counts when you need pre-aggregated customer-level metrics (counts of orders/payments per customer). payments_core differs by providing raw payment rows and not aggregated customer-level metrics. | use seller_revenue_rolling when you need time-windowed rolling revenue metrics per seller (pre-aggregated and windowed). payments_core differs because it contains raw payment entries without rolling/window computations.

views.description: Payment attempts per order preserving sequential index, type, installments and value. Useful for payment-method analytics and joining to orders. | Use for: payment method distribution and amounts; analysis of multi-part payments (installments); join payments to orders for revenue reconciliation

views.name: products_core
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  product_id,
  product_category_name,
  product_name_lenght,
  product_description_lenght,
  product_photos_qty,
  product_weight_g,
  product_length_cm,
  product_height_cm,
  product_width_cm
FROM olist_products

params.description: Provides one-row-per-product descriptive attributes and physical dimensions for products in the olist_products table.
params.when_to_use: Looking up product descriptive attributes (category name, name length, description length) for a given product_id. | Reporting or filtering on product physical characteristics (weight_g, length_cm, height_cm, width_cm) at the product level. | Joining product-level attributes into analyses where products are the primary grain (e.g., product catalogs, product-level joins to aggregated sales).
params.when_not_to_use: Joining directly to order-line or order-level tables when you need correct aggregated sales/quantity revenue measures without handling duplication — products_core is one-row-per-product, so joining it to a many-order-items table is safe, but joining an order-level aggregate to a many-product-per-order relation without re-aggregation can mis-count. | Attempting to use this view to answer transactional questions such as 'how many times a product was ordered' — it contains no order or sales counts; using it for counts will produce silently wrong results (grain mismatch). | Using product attribute columns as pre-aggregated metrics (e.g., summing product_weight_g across products as if it were total shipped weight) without confirming the desired aggregation and deduplication rules — summing across products is product-level total, not order-shipment total, and will be incorrect if you need shipment-weight which depends on order quantities.
params.output_schema: product_id: Unique product identifier — derived directly from olist_products.product_id. | product_category_name: Product category name string — derived directly from olist_products.product_category_name. | product_name_lenght: Length of the product name (as stored) — derived directly from olist_products.product_name_lenght. | product_description_lenght: Length of the product description (as stored) — derived directly from olist_products.product_description_lenght. | product_photos_qty: Number of product photos (as stored) — derived directly from olist_products.product_photos_qty. | product_weight_g: Product weight in grams (as stored) — derived directly from olist_products.product_weight_g. | product_length_cm: Product length in centimeters (as stored) — derived directly from olist_products.product_length_cm. | product_height_cm: Product height in centimeters (as stored) — derived directly from olist_products.product_height_cm. | product_width_cm: Product width in centimeters (as stored) — derived directly from olist_products.product_width_cm.
params.grounded_columns: olist_products.product_id | olist_products.product_category_name | olist_products.product_name_lenght | olist_products.product_description_lenght | olist_products.product_photos_qty | olist_products.product_weight_g | olist_products.product_length_cm | olist_products.product_height_cm | olist_products.product_width_cm
params.metric: product_id = direct column (no aggregation) | product_category_name = direct column (no aggregation) | product_name_lenght = direct column (no aggregation) | product_description_lenght = direct column (no aggregation) | product_photos_qty = direct column (no aggregation) | product_weight_g = direct column (no aggregation) | product_length_cm = direct column (no aggregation) | product_height_cm = direct column (no aggregation) | product_width_cm = direct column (no aggregation)
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to order_items_core on order_items_core.product_id = products_core.product_id — safe because products_core is one-row-per-product; joining to the order_items one-to-many table will replicate the product attributes across order items but will not duplicate per-product measures (there are no aggregated product measures in this view to be inflated). | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to product_category_translation on product_category_translation.product_category_name = products_core.product_category_name — safe if product_category_name is one-to-one in translation; verify translation table cardinality to avoid duplicates. | do NOT join products_core directly to any aggregated view that represents a different grain (e.g., customer_order_counts) without aligning grain — joining a product-level view to a per-customer aggregation will create a cross-join-like multiplication unless joined through an intermediate key (there is no customer_id here). | do NOT join products_core to any many-to-many product grouping or tagging table without first aggregating tags (e.g., tag lists) to one row per product, because that would multiply rows per product and could incorrectly inflate downstream counts if you then aggregate without deduplication. | When merging with orders_core or payments_core: prefer joining via order_items_core (order_items_core.product_id -> products_core.product_id and order_items_core.order_id -> orders_core.order_id) so that product attributes are attached at the order-item grain; directly joining products_core to orders_core is meaningless (no common key) and will produce cross joins if misused.
params.comparison: use product_category_translation instead when you need normalized or translated category labels — product_category_translation specializes in mapping category names to normalized values; products_core only exposes the raw product_category_name from olist_products. | use order_items_core when you need product-level sales metrics (quantity ordered, price, subtotal) because order_items_core contains transactional measures per order line; products_core contains only static product attributes and no sales measures. | use orders_with_items_payments when you need a ready-joined view that combines orders, their items and payments at the order-item grain — that view already handles joining order_items to orders/payments and is safer for transactional analyses than manually joining products_core to multiple transactional tables without re-aggregation.

views.description: Product dimension at one row per product with descriptive and size/weight measures. Use for product-level aggregation and joins. | Use for: product sizing and weight distributions; category-level sales when joined to order items; product enrichment and translations

views.name: customers_core
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  customer_id,
  customer_unique_id,
  customer_zip_code_prefix,
  customer_city,
  customer_state
FROM olist_customers

params.description: Canonical one-row-per-customer table: basic customer identifiers and location (zip/city/state).
params.when_to_use: Look up a customer's canonical identifiers (customer_id and customer_unique_id). | Enrich orders or other events with customer-level attributes (zip code prefix, city, state) when joining on customer_id. | Report counts or metrics grouped by customer attributes after ensuring measures are aggregated at order/item/payment level first.
params.when_not_to_use: Joining directly to order_items_core, payments_core, or orders_with_items_payments to compute sums/counts without re-aggregation — will cause double-counting because those are one-to-many relative to customers. | Using this view as a source of temporal customer snapshots or cohorts — it is static/current customer attributes (no history/timestamp) and does not represent cohort membership over time. | Expecting any aggregated measures (orders, revenue, item counts) to be present — this view contains only customer attributes, not metrics; mixing metrics here without re-aggregation is a grain mismatch.
params.output_schema: customer_id: Unique customer identifier (from olist_customers.customer_id). This is the primary key/grain of this view. | customer_unique_id: Business-level customer identifier possibly repeated across multiple customer_id rows (from olist_customers.customer_unique_id). | customer_zip_code_prefix: Customer ZIP code prefix / postal area (from olist_customers.customer_zip_code_prefix). | customer_city: Customer city name (from olist_customers.customer_city). | customer_state: Customer state abbreviation (from olist_customers.customer_state).
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE: join to orders_core on olist_customers.customer_id = orders_core.customer_id — safe for adding order-level columns only if you do NOT aggregate order-level measures into this view; joining orders_core (one-to-many) to this one-row-per-customer view is safe when you intend to expand customers into their orders, but will multiply customer rows as expected. | cardinality-SAFE: join to sellers_core, product_category_translation, or geolocation_zip_median when joining on keys that are one-to-one (e.g., seller_id to sellers_core) — these joins do not multiply customer rows if the join key is unique on the right-hand side. | DO NOT join customers_core directly to order_items_core, payments_core, or orders_with_items_payments if you intend to produce customer-level aggregates (e.g., total revenue per customer) without first aggregating the one-to-many side to customer level (e.g., sum(amount) GROUP BY customer_id). Such joins would duplicate customer rows and produce inflated measures. | If you need customer-level metrics (order counts, revenue), use customer_order_counts (aggregated per customer) or aggregate orders_core/order_items_core/payments_core to customer_id before joining to this view. Example safe pattern: LEFT JOIN (SELECT customer_id, SUM(payment_value) AS total_paid FROM payments_core GROUP BY customer_id) AS p USING(customer_id).
params.comparison: use customer_order_counts instead when you need pre-computed customer-level aggregates (order counts, totals) — customer_order_counts is an AGG view that provides metrics at the same customer grain. | use orders_core or orders_with_items_payments when you need order- or order-item-level detail (transactions) rather than one-row-per-customer attributes — those views carry the higher-cardinality transactional grain. | use geolocation_zip_median when you need aggregated geographic metrics (e.g., median values by zip) rather than raw customer zip codes — geolocation_zip_median is an AGG view keyed by zip and provides derived statistics.

views.description: Customer dimension: one row per customer preserving both internal id and customer_unique_id and location attributes for geospatial/cohort analysis. | Use for: customer location distribution; repeat-customer analysis using customer_unique_id; join customers to orders for CRM metrics

views.name: sellers_core
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  seller_id,
  seller_zip_code_prefix,
  seller_city,
  seller_state
FROM olist_sellers

params.description: Provides one-row-per-seller core reference information (seller id and location fields) for lookups and joins.
params.when_to_use: Lookup seller attributes (zip, city, state) for a given seller_id or set of seller_ids. | Join seller descriptive attributes into analyses that are at the seller grain without changing measure counts. | Build dashboards, filters or labels that need seller location metadata.
params.when_not_to_use: Joining directly to transactional tables (orders, order_items, payments, etc.) when you intend to aggregate measures — doing so without re-aggregation can produce incorrect counts because those tables are one-to-many relative to sellers. | Using it as the source of seller-level metrics (revenue, order counts) — this view contains only descriptive columns (no aggregated measures); mixing it with metrics requires joining to an aggregated metric view (or aggregating after join). | Attempting to compute time-based cohorts or rolling metrics here — the view is static per seller and contains no time dimension; using it for cohorting will lose time granularity and produce silently wrong cohorts.
params.output_schema: seller_id: Unique identifier for a seller — sourced from olist_sellers.seller_id | seller_zip_code_prefix: Seller postal code prefix (location attribute) — sourced from olist_sellers.seller_zip_code_prefix | seller_city: Seller city name (location attribute) — sourced from olist_sellers.seller_city | seller_state: Seller state/region code (location attribute) — sourced from olist_sellers.seller_state
params.metric: This view exposes no derived metrics or aggregates; all output columns are direct passthroughs from base columns.
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to orders_core on seller_id — safe because sellers_core is one-row-per-seller and orders_core is one-to-many (orders). Joining sellers_core as the dimension will not duplicate seller attributes, but measures from orders_core remain at order grain. Always aggregate measures from orders_core after joining if you want seller-level measures. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to customer-facing dimension views (customers_core) on nothing — there is no natural key; do not attempt to join unless you have an explicit key relationship. | do NOT join sellers_core directly to order_items_core, payments_core, or orders_with_items_payments expecting unchanged seller-level measures — these are one-to-many relative to sellers and will multiply rows. Instead, either: (a) aggregate those transactional tables to seller_id first (e.g., SUM(amount) GROUP BY seller_id) and then join, or (b) join and then re-aggregate to seller_id, ensuring you apply appropriate DISTINCT or SUM of metrics as required. | do NOT join sellers_core to geolocation_zip_median or other AGG views without checking grain compatibility — if geolocation_zip_median is aggregated by zip code, join on seller_zip_code_prefix is okay (one-to-one or many-to-one) only if that AGG is at the same zip-code grain; otherwise aggregate appropriately before joining.
params.comparison: use orders_with_items_payments instead when you need combined transactional rows (orders with items and payments) at the order/item/payment grain — that view contains transactional measures and joins that this view does not provide. | use customer_order_counts when you need pre-aggregated seller metrics derived from orders/customers (if such a sibling produces seller-level aggregates); sellers_core only contains descriptive attributes and no counts or sums. | use geolocation_zip_median when you need aggregated location statistics by zip (e.g., median coordinates) — sellers_core provides only the raw zip code prefix, not aggregated geo metrics.

views.description: Seller dimension: one row per seller with location attributes for seller-level summaries and joins. | Use for: seller geographic distribution; seller performance when joined to order_items/orders

views.name: geolocation_zip_median
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  geolocation_zip_code_prefix,
  AVG(geolocation_lat) AS geolocation_lat,
  AVG(geolocation_lng) AS geolocation_lng,
  COUNT(*) AS sample_count
FROM olist_geolocation
GROUP BY geolocation_zip_code_prefix

params.description: Provides per-zip-code-prefix geographic centroids (average latitude/longitude) and the sample count of geolocation rows used to compute them.
params.when_to_use: When you need a single representative latitude/longitude for each geolocation_zip_code_prefix (e.g., to plot zip-prefix centroids on a map). | When you need to know how many raw geolocation samples contributed to each zip-prefix centroid (data quality / weighting). | When joining a geographic centroid (one row per geolocation_zip_code_prefix) to other aggregated views or dimension tables at the same zip-code-prefix grain.
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use this view to represent individual address points or to preserve within-zip variation — the view returns averages and loses per-row detail (grain mismatch). | Do not join this view directly to lower-grain, one-to-many datasets (for example order_items_core or orders_with_items_payments) expecting counts or sums to remain correct — joining to a multi-row-per-zip table will duplicate rows and silently inflate metrics unless you re-aggregate after the join. | Do not treat sample_count as a global unique entity count (e.g., number of customers or orders) — sample_count is COUNT(*) of olist_geolocation rows for that zip prefix, not counts from other tables (cohort/metric-misinterpretation). | Do not use the averaged latitude/longitude as a precise location for distance-sensitive calculations (e.g., routing or precise geospatial joins) because averaging coordinates is an approximation and may be misleading for large or irregular areas.
params.output_schema: geolocation_zip_code_prefix: zip-code prefix key used to group rows — derived from olist_geolocation.geolocation_zip_code_prefix | geolocation_lat: mean latitude across all olist_geolocation rows with the same geolocation_zip_code_prefix — derived from AVG(olist_geolocation.geolocation_lat) | geolocation_lng: mean longitude across all olist_geolocation rows with the same geolocation_zip_code_prefix — derived from AVG(olist_geolocation.geolocation_lng) | sample_count: number of olist_geolocation rows aggregated into the centroid for this geolocation_zip_code_prefix — derived from COUNT(*) over olist_geolocation grouped by geolocation_zip_code_prefix
params.metric: geolocation_lat = AVG(olist_geolocation.geolocation_lat) | geolocation_lng = AVG(olist_geolocation.geolocation_lng) | sample_count = COUNT(*)  -- count of olist_geolocation rows per geolocation_zip_code_prefix
params.composition: Cardinality-SAFE: join to a dimension that is one-row-per-zip-prefix (e.g., a zip-prefix lookup table) on geolocation_zip_code_prefix — safe because this view already has one row per geolocation_zip_code_prefix so measures are not duplicated. | Cardinality-SAFE: join to sibling aggregated views that are also one-row-per-geolocation_zip_code_prefix (if available) on geolocation_zip_code_prefix — safe because keys align 1:1. | UNSAFE: do NOT join this view directly to orders_core, order_items_core, orders_with_items_payments, customers_core, sellers_core, or any other table/view that has potentially many rows per geolocation_zip_code_prefix without re-aggregating after the join — those joins will multiply rows and therefore multiply sample_count and any derived measures, causing silently incorrect totals. | UNSAFE: do NOT join and then SUM(this.sample_count) expecting it to represent unique entities across the joined result unless you first ensure the join preserves one row per geolocation_zip_code_prefix or you deduplicate/re-aggregate on geolocation_zip_code_prefix after the join. | If you must combine with a one-to-many table, either: (a) aggregate the one-to-many side to one row per geolocation_zip_code_prefix before joining, or (b) join and then re-aggregate by geolocation_zip_code_prefix in the downstream query to restore correct counts/averages.
params.comparison: use orders_core instead when you need order-level attributes (orders_core is normalized at order grain) — geolocation_zip_median has geographic centroids only and is at zip-prefix grain, not order grain. | use customers_core when you need customer-level attributes or customer counts — sample_count here counts geolocation rows, not unique customers. | use orders_with_items_payments when you need combined order/item/payment measures across orders — that view joins multiple tables and provides order-related aggregates, whereas geolocation_zip_median only provides averaged coordinates and counts from the geolocation table. | use order_review_summary or latest_review_per_order when you need review metrics — those sibling views are about reviews and orders and have different grain and measures than geographic centroids. | This view differs from seller_revenue_rolling and customer_order_counts in that it is purely geographic aggregation (latitude/longitude averages and sample counts) and contains no revenue, order, or customer-level metrics; prefer those sibling views when your question is about revenue or order counts rather than geography.

views.description: Aggregated geolocation per zip prefix: median latitude/longitude and a sample count. Use to map zip prefixes to a representative lat/lng. | Use for: map customers/sellers to lat/lng by zip prefix; visualization of geographic distribution of orders or customers

views.name: orders_with_items_payments
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  o.order_id,
  o.customer_id,
  o.order_status,
  o.order_purchase_timestamp,
  oi.order_item_id,
  oi.product_id,
  oi.seller_id,
  oi.price,
  oi.freight_value,
  p.payment_sequential,
  p.payment_type,
  p.payment_installments,
  p.payment_value
FROM olist_orders o
LEFT JOIN olist_order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
LEFT JOIN olist_order_payments p ON o.order_id = p.order_id

params.description: Rows at the combined order-item-payment level: each row represents a single order item together with a single payment record for the same order (grain: order_id, order_item_id, payment_sequential).
params.when_to_use: Analyze payments in relation to individual order items when you intentionally want a Cartesian pairing of order items and payments for the same order (e.g., inspect every combination of item × payment for an order). | Build datasets that need item-level attributes (product_id, seller_id, price) alongside payment attributes (payment_type, payment_installments, payment_value) for the same order. | Debug or explore how payments align with items for a specific order_id or to check inconsistencies between item totals and payments.
params.when_not_to_use: Summarizing order-level metrics (total order revenue, total payments, number of payments per order) — WHY: this view repeats order rows for each order_item × payment combination, so summing price or payment_value will overcount unless you first deduplicate/aggregate to the intended grain. | Customer- or order-cohort analyses that expect one row per order or per customer — WHY: the grain is finer (item × payment), so cohort counts and rates (e.g., conversion, average order value per customer) will be wrong unless you aggregate correctly. | Any join that expects measures to be additive at order_id or customer_id without first aggregating out the item/payment multiplicity — WHY: joining to additional one-to-many tables will multiply rows further and silently inflate metrics.
params.output_schema: order_id: order identifier — derived from olist_orders.order_id (o.order_id) in the FROM clause | customer_id: customer identifier for the order — derived from olist_orders.customer_id (o.customer_id) | order_status: status of the order (e.g., delivered, shipped) — derived from olist_orders.order_status (o.order_status) | order_purchase_timestamp: timestamp when the order was placed — derived from olist_orders.order_purchase_timestamp (o.order_purchase_timestamp) | order_item_id: identifier for the specific item line within the order — derived from olist_order_items.order_item_id (oi.order_item_id) | product_id: product identifier for the order item — derived from olist_order_items.product_id (oi.product_id) | seller_id: seller identifier for the order item — derived from olist_order_items.seller_id (oi.seller_id) | price: item price for the order item (single-line price) — derived from olist_order_items.price (oi.price) | freight_value: shipping/freight charge for the order item — derived from olist_order_items.freight_value (oi.freight_value) | payment_sequential: ordinal number of the payment for the order (1 = first payment, 2 = second, ...) — derived from olist_order_payments.payment_sequential (p.payment_sequential) | payment_type: payment method used (e.g., credit_card) — derived from olist_order_payments.payment_type (p.payment_type) | payment_installments: number of installments for that payment — derived from olist_order_payments.payment_installments (p.payment_installments) | payment_value: monetary value applied in that payment row — derived from olist_order_payments.payment_value (p.payment_value)
params.grounded_columns: olist_orders.order_id | olist_orders.customer_id | olist_orders.order_status | olist_orders.order_purchase_timestamp | olist_order_items.order_id | olist_order_items.order_item_id | olist_order_items.product_id | olist_order_items.seller_id | olist_order_items.price | olist_order_items.freight_value | olist_order_payments.order_id | olist_order_payments.payment_sequential | olist_order_payments.payment_type | olist_order_payments.payment_installments | olist_order_payments.payment_value
params.metric: price = direct column copy (oi.price) — not an aggregate in this view | freight_value = direct column copy (oi.freight_value) — not an aggregate in this view | payment_value = direct column copy (p.payment_value) — not an aggregate in this view | There are no aggregated metrics in this view; all outputs are base columns projected at the view's grain (order_id, order_item_id, payment_sequential). Any aggregate (SUM/COUNT/AVG) must be performed by the consumer after choosing and clearly specifying the desired aggregation grain.
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE: join to dimensions that are one-row-per-key such as products_core on product_id — join: this_view.product_id = products_core.product_id — safe because products_core is expected to be one row per product_id and will not duplicate rows or measures. | cardinality-SAFE: join to sellers_core on seller_id — join: this_view.seller_id = sellers_core.seller_id — safe because sellers_core is one-row-per-seller. | DO NOT join without aggregation to payments_core or order_items_core if you expect to preserve additive measures at order or customer grain — reason: payments_core or order_items_core are one-to-many relative to orders; joining another one-to-many will multiply rows (e.g., joining another payment table or another item-level view will produce item × payment × other multiplicity). | DO NOT join this view to other one-to-many views on order_id (for example, joining to order_review_summary or customer_order_counts) without first aggregating one side to a stable grain — reason: this view already expands orders to item × payment rows; additional one-to-many joins will silently duplicate payment_value and price, causing overcounts. | If you need order-level totals, first aggregate this view to order_id (e.g., SUM(price) per order_item_id deduplicated or aggregate items to order-level then join payments aggregated to order-level), or better: use orders_core + aggregated payments/order_items to avoid multiplicative expansion. | To combine with latest_review_per_order (one-row-per-order): safe if you join on order_id but only after you aggregate this view to the order-level (otherwise the latest_review_per_order row will be repeated for each item × payment).
params.comparison: use orders_core instead when you need one-row-per-order (orders_core has the order-level grain; this view expands to item×payment and will overcount order-level aggregates). | use order_items_core instead when you need one-row-per-order_item without payment duplication (order_items_core provides item-level rows; this view will duplicate items for each payment of the same order). | use payments_core instead when you need one-row-per-payment without item duplication (payments_core provides payment-level rows; this view duplicates payments for each item on the order). | use customer_order_counts when you need aggregated customer-level counts/metrics (this view is too granular and will require aggregation to match the sibling's aggregates). | use latest_review_per_order when you specifically need the single most-relevant review per order (this view will repeat that single review if joined without aggregation because it has multiple rows per order).

views.description: Denormalized order-item-payment relation: one row per order_item preserving order, item, product and payment attributes. Useful for revenue attribution and per-item payment analysis. Note: joining payments multiplies rows; payments are kept at their sequential level. | Use for: per-item revenue by payment method; analysis of orders with multiple payments or items; seller revenue by payment type

views.name: order_review_summary
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  order_id,
  COUNT(review_id) AS review_count,
  AVG(review_score) AS review_score_avg,
  MAX(review_creation_date) AS review_last_created_at
FROM olist_order_reviews
GROUP BY order_id

params.description: Per-order aggregated summary of review activity: count, average score, and most recent review timestamp for each order_id.
params.when_to_use: When you need one row per order to report how many reviews that order received, the average review score for that order, or the most recent review timestamp for that order. | When joining order-level review metrics into order-level analyses (e.g., join to orders_core) without changing the aggregation. | When filtering or aggregating at the order grain (e.g., compute distribution of review_count across orders).
params.when_not_to_use: Joining this view to order_items_core or any other one-to-many child of orders without re-aggregation: doing so will multiply rows and therefore multiply review_count and distort averages and maxima. | Using this view to answer customer-level or seller-level questions directly (e.g., reviews per customer) without first rolling up to the desired higher grain — otherwise you risk double-counting orders when customers have multiple orders. | Using review_count as a proxy for distinct reviewers or distinct review events if the downstream join introduces duplicates — COUNT(review_id) here is valid only at the order grain in isolation. | Using this view when you need the latest single review row per order with all review attributes (text, reviewer id). For that use latest_review_per_order (RANK) which preserves a single ranked row rather than aggregates.
params.output_schema: order_id: The order identifier (source: olist_order_reviews.order_id). This is the grouping key; one row per order_id. | review_count: Number of reviews for the order (source aggregate: COUNT(review_id) over rows in olist_order_reviews for that order_id). | review_score_avg: Average review score for the order (source aggregate: AVG(review_score) over rows in olist_order_reviews for that order_id). | review_last_created_at: Timestamp/date of the most recent review for the order (source aggregate: MAX(review_creation_date) over rows in olist_order_reviews for that order_id).
params.metric: review_count = COUNT(olist_order_reviews.review_id) grouped by olist_order_reviews.order_id | review_score_avg = AVG(olist_order_reviews.review_score) grouped by olist_order_reviews.order_id | review_last_created_at = MAX(olist_order_reviews.review_creation_date) grouped by olist_order_reviews.order_id
params.composition: Cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to orders_core on order_id — safe because this view is one-row-per-order_id, and orders_core is one-row-per-order_id, so measures are not duplicated. | Cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to customers_core on customer_id only after joining orders_core (orders_core -> customers_core) or by first joining orders_core to this view on order_id. Do not join this view directly to customers_core without an order join if you do not preserve order_id as the key. | Do NOT join this view directly to order_items_core, products_core, or any other table that is one-to-many with orders (e.g., order_items_core has multiple rows per order_id): such joins will duplicate this view's rows and therefore multiply review_count and distort review_score_avg and review_last_created_at. If you must combine with a one-to-many detail, either aggregate that detail to order_id first or re-aggregate after the join to preserve correct order-level measures. | Do NOT join this aggregate view to latest_review_per_order and then aggregate again to order: latest_review_per_order is a single-row-per-order representation of the latest review (RANK); if you need both aggregated metrics and latest review attributes, prefer joining latest_review_per_order (which is 1:1 with this view on order_id) — that join is safe because both are one-row-per-order_id. | When composing into higher-grain metrics (e.g., customer-level), aggregate this view's review_count using SUM(review_count) grouped by customer after joining via orders_core to avoid mis-counts; do not attempt to AVG(review_score_avg) across orders as a replacement for a true overall average unless you weight by review_count: overall_avg_score = SUM(review_score_avg * review_count) / SUM(review_count).
params.comparison: use latest_review_per_order instead when you need attributes of the most recent review row (text, reviewer id) for each order — latest_review_per_order preserves row-level review attributes via ranking rather than aggregating. | use customer_order_counts when the desired grain is customer-level order counts rather than order-level review metrics; customer_order_counts is aggregated at the customer grain and already handles order-level to customer-level rollups. | use orders_with_items_payments when you need combined order, items, and payment information together; that view joins multiple tables and is intended for analyzing orders with their items/payments, whereas order_review_summary strictly summarizes reviews at the order grain.

views.description: One row per order summarizing review metrics: average and count of review_score and latest review timestamp. Use for joining order sentiment to orders or customers. | Use for: order sentiment and review coverage; join review aggregates to orders/customers for NPS-like metrics

views.name: product_category_translation
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  p.product_id,
  p.product_category_name,
  t.product_category_name_english
FROM olist_products p
LEFT JOIN product_category_name_translation t ON p.product_category_name = t.product_category_name

params.description: Provides product-level rows mapping each product_id's product_category_name to an English category name (translation lookup).
params.when_to_use: Look up the English translation for a product's category when analyzing products at the product_id grain. | Enrich a product-level dataset (one row per product_id) with a normalized English product category label for reporting or downstream joins. | Filtering or grouping products by translated category labels (English) while preserving one row per product.
params.when_not_to_use: Joining this view directly into order- or order_item-level analyses when you need order- or item-level counts/amounts — doing so without care can duplicate product-level rows per order item and overcount (grain mismatch). | Using this view as if it were an aggregated product_category-level summary (cohort) — it is one row per product_id, not aggregated by category, so metrics like product counts per category must be computed explicitly (e.g., COUNT(DISTINCT product_id) or GROUP BY product_category_name_english). | Assuming a translation exists for every product_category_name — the LEFT JOIN preserves products whose category lacks a translation resulting in NULL product_category_name_english; treating NULL as a valid label without handling will silently mis-classify those rows. | Joining multiple translation sources or joining translations then aggregating without re-checking uniqueness of translation keys — if product_category_name_translation had duplicate keys (multiple rows per product_category_name), joins would duplicate products. The SQL assumes product_category_name_translation.product_category_name is unique.
params.output_schema: product_id: product identifier for the product (source: olist_products.product_id). Grain: one row per product_id. | product_category_name: original product category label in the product record (source: olist_products.product_category_name). | product_category_name_english: translated English product category label (source: product_category_name_translation.product_category_name_english). NULL if no translation exists.
params.metric: This view contains no aggregated metrics. All output columns are direct projections/lookup results, not aggregates. | If you need counts derived from this view, compute them explicitly, e.g.: num_products = COUNT(DISTINCT product_id) or products_per_translation = COUNT(*) GROUP BY product_category_name_english
params.composition: Cardinality-SAFE: join to product-level dimensions or lookups keyed by product_id (for example, join to products_core on product_id) — safe because this view is one row per product_id, so product-level measures will not be multiplied. | Cardinality-UNSAFE: do NOT join this view directly to order_items_core or orders_core (one-to-many from products to order items/orders) if you intend to sum or count order-level measures without re-aggregation. That would duplicate product rows per matching order/order_item and overcount. | When enriching order- or item-level data with product_category_name_english, join from the order/item side to this view on product_id (order_items_core.product_id = product_category_translation.product_id). This preserves the order-level cardinality because you are attaching product attributes to each item; however, if you then aggregate back to product_id you must deduplicate as needed. | If you need to join to any table that is many-to-one into products (e.g., a table that has multiple translations per category), ensure the join key on product_category_name_translation is unique (product_category_name) or pre-aggregate/deduplicate translation table to a single row per product_category_name to avoid silently multiplying rows.
params.comparison: use products_core instead when you need a fuller canonical product record (products_core likely contains more product attributes and normalized fields) — product_category_translation only adds the English translation and preserves product-level grain. | use geolocation_zip_median or other AGG sibling views when you require aggregated metrics (e.g., median values by zip) rather than raw product-level lookup rows. | use orders_with_items_payments when your primary analysis is order-centered and you need combined order + item + payment rows; in that case attach product_category_translation via product_id to the order_items component rather than replacing order-level joins.

views.description: Map product category codes to English names. One row per product_id with both original and english category when available. Useful for readable category-level reporting. | Use for: category-level sales with readable category names; translate product_category_name for dashboards and exports

views.name: customer_order_counts
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  customer_id,
  COUNT(order_id) AS orders_count,
  MIN(order_purchase_timestamp) AS first_order_purchase_timestamp,
  MAX(order_purchase_timestamp) AS last_order_purchase_timestamp
FROM olist_orders
GROUP BY customer_id

params.description: Per-customer order summary: total count of orders and first/last order purchase timestamps for each customer_id.
params.when_to_use: Get how many orders each customer has placed (orders_count) and the timestamps of their first and last purchases. | Filter customers by recency (first/last order timestamp) or by having at least N orders. | Join a one-row-per-customer dimension (e.g., customers_core) to enrich customer-level attributes without changing aggregates.
params.when_not_to_use: Joining directly to order_items_core, products_core, or any order-level / item-level table expecting counts to remain accurate — doing so creates a one-to-many multiplication and will over-count orders_count. | Using this view to analyze order-level details (order_id-specific metrics) — the view is aggregated to customer granularity and has lost per-order identity. | Using this view as-is to compute per-customer revenue or item counts — orders_count is just a count of orders, not a sum of payments or items; you must join and re-aggregate from payments_core or order_items_core to get revenue or item counts. | Treating MIN/MAX timestamps as cohort assignment without confirming timezone/partitioning: they reflect order_purchase_timestamp values in olist_orders and may need normalization if you compare with other timestamp fields.
params.output_schema: customer_id: unique identifier of the customer (derived from olist_orders.customer_id). | orders_count: total number of orders for that customer (derived from COUNT(order_id) over rows in olist_orders grouped by customer_id). | first_order_purchase_timestamp: earliest order_purchase_timestamp for that customer (derived from MIN(order_purchase_timestamp) in olist_orders grouped by customer_id). | last_order_purchase_timestamp: latest order_purchase_timestamp for that customer (derived from MAX(order_purchase_timestamp) in olist_orders grouped by customer_id).
params.metric: orders_count = COUNT(order_id)  -- count of distinct order rows per customer as present in olist_orders (note: COUNT(order_id) counts non-null order_id rows; if order_id is unique per row this equals number of orders). | first_order_purchase_timestamp = MIN(order_purchase_timestamp)  -- earliest purchase timestamp per customer from olist_orders. | last_order_purchase_timestamp = MAX(order_purchase_timestamp)  -- latest purchase timestamp per customer from olist_orders.
params.composition: Cardinality-SAFE: join to customers_core on customer_id — customers_core is a one-row-per-customer dimension, so joining preserves this view's measures without duplication. | Cardinality-SAFE: join to any other one-row-per-customer view (or projection) on customer_id — safe because this view is one-row-per-customer. | Do NOT join directly to orders_core, order_items_core, payments_core, or products_core without re-aggregating those tables to customer granularity first — these are one-to-many relative to customer and will multiply orders_count and distort first/last timestamps if joined at a finer grain. | If you need to combine with order-level metrics (e.g., revenue from payments_core), first aggregate those metrics to customer_id (e.g., SUM(payment_value) GROUP BY customer_id in payments_core) and then join the aggregated result to this view on customer_id to avoid double-counting. | If joining to orders_with_items_payments or other pre-joined/order-level JOIN views, ensure that that view is either pre-aggregated to customer_id or used in a subquery that groups by customer_id before joining; otherwise measures will be duplicated.
params.comparison: use orders_core instead when you need order-level detail (order_id, order_status, timestamps) — orders_core preserves row-level orders whereas customer_order_counts is aggregated to customer grain. | use orders_with_items_payments when you need a combined order-level dataset that includes item and payment details — but aggregate that view to customer_id before replacing customer_order_counts. | use order_review_summary or latest_review_per_order when you need review-level aggregates tied to orders — join those summaries to orders_core and then aggregate to customer to combine with this view safely. | use seller_revenue_rolling or geolocation_zip_median when you need rolling revenue or location-level medians — these are different grains (time/window or zip-level) and should be joined only after aligning grain (e.g., aggregate to customer or map customers to zips and aggregate appropriately).

views.description: Customer-level order counts and first/last purchase timestamps. One row per customer (customer_id). Useful for retention, recency and frequency analyses. | Use for: RFM/recency-frequency analyses; cohorting customers by first purchase

views.name: latest_review_per_order
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  review_id,
  order_id,
  review_score,
  review_comment_title,
  review_comment_message,
  review_creation_date,
  review_answer_timestamp,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY review_creation_date DESC) AS review_rank
FROM olist_order_reviews

params.description: For each review (granularity = review_id), returns the latest review per order with its row-number rank (1 = newest review for that order).
params.when_to_use: Get the most recent review record for each order (filter review_rank = 1). | Analyze review-level attributes (score, text, timestamps) while optionally restricting to the latest review per order. | Join review attributes to order-level records when you want at most one review row per order (after filtering to review_rank = 1).
params.when_not_to_use: Joining this view directly to order_items_core or products_core without first restricting to review_rank = 1 — WHY: this view is at review_id grain and can contain multiple reviews per order; joining to order-level or item-level rows without deduplicating reviews or re-aggregating will produce duplicated measures or overstated counts. | Using review_rank as a cohort or time-window aggregate without applying a filter (e.g., SELECT AVG(review_score) FROM latest_review_per_order) — WHY: as-is the view contains every review (one row per review_id) with a computed rank per order; aggregate results will reflect all reviews, not only latest, unless you filter by review_rank = 1. | Treating review_rank as a stable persistent identifier across re-materializations — WHY: ROW_NUMBER() is computed at query time based on review_creation_date; ties or changes in underlying data can change ranks. | Expecting this view to represent order-level metrics (e.g., one-row-per-order totals) without filtering to the latest per order — WHY: its grain is review_id; order-level aggregates must be derived by grouping or by selecting review_rank = 1.
params.output_schema: review_id: unique identifier for the review (source: olist_order_reviews.review_id). | order_id: identifier of the order this review is associated with (source: olist_order_reviews.order_id). | review_score: numeric score given in the review (source: olist_order_reviews.review_score). | review_comment_title: short title/headline of the review (source: olist_order_reviews.review_comment_title). | review_comment_message: full text message of the review (source: olist_order_reviews.review_comment_message). | review_creation_date: timestamp or date when the review was created (source: olist_order_reviews.review_creation_date). | review_answer_timestamp: timestamp when the seller answered the review, if present (source: olist_order_reviews.review_answer_timestamp). | review_rank: ROW_NUMBER() over (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY review_creation_date DESC) — integer rank of the review within its order, with 1 representing the latest review for that order (derived column).
params.metric: review_rank = ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY review_creation_date DESC)
params.composition: Cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to orders_core on latest_review_per_order.order_id = orders_core.order_id — safe ONLY after you first filter this view to review_rank = 1 so joins do not duplicate latest-review rows. | Safe to join to customers_core on orders_core.customer_id = customers_core.customer_id when the pipeline is: latest_review_per_order (filtered review_rank = 1) -> join to orders_core (one-to-one on order_id) -> join to customers_core (one-to-one on customer_id). The flow preserves one review row per order. | Do NOT join this view directly to order_items_core or products_core (one-to-many from order -> items/products) without re-aggregating reviews or restricting to a single review per order, because order_items_core has multiple rows per order and would multiply review rows/metrics (mis-count). | If you need to combine review-level details with item-level aggregates, first derive a one-row-per-order review set (e.g., SELECT * FROM latest_review_per_order WHERE review_rank = 1) or aggregate the joined result back to order level (e.g., GROUP BY order_id) to avoid double-counting. | Joining to aggregated sibling views (e.g., order_review_summary or customer_order_counts) is safe when those siblings are one-row-per-order or one-row-per-customer respectively and you align the join keys and grains appropriately.
params.comparison: use order_review_summary instead when you need order-level aggregated metrics about reviews (e.g., count of reviews per order, average score per order) — it is an AGG view built for order-level summaries, whereas latest_review_per_order is at the review_id grain and provides raw review rows plus a per-order rank. | use orders_with_items_payments when you need enriched order-level data joined to items and payments — that JOIN view is designed for combining order, item, and payment data; do not replace it with latest_review_per_order which contains review rows and would need deduplication before joining to items to avoid multiplication. | use customer_order_counts when your focus is customer-level aggregates (orders per customer) rather than raw review rows; latest_review_per_order would need aggregation to be comparable.

views.description: Latest review per order using review_creation_date. One row per order for the most recent review. Use to attach the latest textual feedback to orders. | Use for: attach latest review to orders; filter to latest review per order by review_rank <= K downstream

views.name: seller_revenue_rolling
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  oi.seller_id,
  o.order_id,
  o.order_purchase_timestamp,
  oi.order_item_id,
  oi.price,
  oi.freight_value,
  (oi.price + COALESCE(oi.freight_value,0)) AS item_total,
  SUM(oi.price + COALESCE(oi.freight_value,0)) OVER (PARTITION BY oi.seller_id ORDER BY o.order_purchase_timestamp ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS seller_revenue_cumulative
FROM olist_order_items oi
LEFT JOIN olist_orders o ON oi.order_id = o.order_id

params.description: Provides per-seller, per-order-item rows with the running (cumulative) revenue for that seller over time (ordered by order_purchase_timestamp).
params.when_to_use: Show a seller's revenue build-up over time at the order-item level (e.g., time-series chart of cumulative seller revenue). | Calculate cumulative seller revenue up to each order_item event (for reporting or per-item labeling). | Join to order-level or item-level tables when you need the running total at the same row-level (order_item).
params.when_not_to_use: Aggregating to seller-day, seller-month or any coarser grain directly from this view without re-aggregation — because this view is at the order_item grain; summing seller_revenue_cumulative across items or orders will produce incorrect, inflated figures (mis-count/aggregation anti-pattern). | Using the cumulative measure as a period-to-period metric (e.g., revenue in month X) — cumulative values are prefix sums, not period deltas; you must subtract cumulative values at boundaries to get period revenue (cohort/aggregation anti-pattern). | Joining to one-to-many tables (e.g., order_reviews, additional item-level enrichment) without first aggregating those tables to the view's grain — direct joins can duplicate rows and therefore multiply item_total and the cumulative progression (cardinality anti-pattern). | Assuming the ordering is deterministic when multiple orders share the exact same order_purchase_timestamp for the same seller — the window ORDER BY uses only timestamp, so ties can produce arbitrary ordering among tied rows and thus nondeterministic cumulative values unless you add tie-breakers.
params.output_schema: seller_id: Identifier of the seller for the order item. Derived from olist_order_items.seller_id. | order_id: Identifier of the order containing the item. Derived from olist_orders.order_id (via join) — same value as olist_order_items.order_id. | order_purchase_timestamp: Timestamp when the order was purchased. Derived from olist_orders.order_purchase_timestamp (used as the ordering key for the running total). | order_item_id: Identifier of the order item (item-level grain). Derived from olist_order_items.order_item_id. | price: Item price charged for this order item. Derived from olist_order_items.price. | freight_value: Freight/shipping cost for this item. Derived from olist_order_items.freight_value (may be NULL). | item_total: Per-item revenue amount = price + COALESCE(freight_value, 0). Computed from olist_order_items.price and olist_order_items.freight_value. | seller_revenue_cumulative: Cumulative sum of item_total for the seller, ordered by order_purchase_timestamp, computed as SUM(price + COALESCE(freight_value,0)) OVER (PARTITION BY seller_id ORDER BY order_purchase_timestamp ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW).
params.grounded_columns: olist_order_items.seller_id | olist_order_items.order_id | olist_order_items.order_item_id | olist_order_items.price | olist_order_items.freight_value | olist_orders.order_id | olist_orders.order_purchase_timestamp
params.metric: item_total = olist_order_items.price + COALESCE(olist_order_items.freight_value, 0) | seller_revenue_cumulative = SUM(olist_order_items.price + COALESCE(olist_order_items.freight_value, 0)) OVER (PARTITION BY olist_order_items.seller_id ORDER BY olist_orders.order_purchase_timestamp ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
params.composition: Safe: Join this view to a seller-level table/view (e.g., sellers_core) ON seller_id — sellers_core is one-row-per-seller, so it will not duplicate the view's rows or distort cumulative amounts. | Safe: Join to orders_core ON order_id if you only need order-level attributes and you expect one order row per order_id. This preserves the per-order-item rows and does not duplicate measures (orders_core is one-row-per-order). | Do NOT join directly to order_review_summary, latest_review_per_order or any other one-to-many table relative to order_item without first aggregating that table to order_item or order_id level — they can multiply rows leading to duplicated item_total and incorrect cumulative values. | Do NOT join to order_items_core or other multi-row item-level sources on seller_id alone — joining additional item-level detail without careful join keys or aggregation will create many-to-many expansions and inflate results. | If you need seller-level aggregated metrics (e.g., total revenue per seller for a period), aggregate this view (or better, aggregate source order_items) to seller and the desired period rather than summing seller_revenue_cumulative. Summing the cumulative column is incorrect because it double-counts prior items.
params.comparison: use order_items_core instead when you only need canonical item-level columns without the running total — order_items_core provides normalized item rows and should be used as the authoritative item grain. | use orders_core when you need pure order-level reporting (one row per order) rather than item-level running totals — orders_core is one-row-per-order and avoids per-item duplication. | use customer_order_counts or geolocation_zip_median when you need aggregated/summary metrics at customer or zip-level respectively; those siblings are aggregated views (AGG) and are appropriate when you want rolled-up numbers rather than per-item cumulative progress. | do not substitute this view for payments_core: payments_core contains payment instrument/amount rows and may be at a different grain; if you need revenue recognized from payments, join and reconcile at matching grains rather than assuming item_total == payment amount.

views.description: Seller-level running total revenue ordered by order purchase timestamp. One row per order_item per seller exposing cumulative revenue; useful for trend and cumulative-share analyses. | Use for: seller cumulative revenue over time; identify sellers reaching revenue milestones
